We launched after 6 months of building.

On day one, almost nobody used it.

Not because the product was broken. Because we solved a problem our users didn't actually have — at least, not in the way we thought they did.

We had validated the *idea* in conversations. We never validated the *behavior*. We asked, "Would you use this?" instead of watching how people solved the problem today, what they paid for, and what they complained about unprompted.

Everyone was polite. No one was desperate.

That launch cost us time, money, and momentum. It taught me a lesson I now repeat to every team I work with:

Fall in love with the problem. Not your solution to it.

Now, before we write a line of code, we test with ugly prototypes, charge money early (even $1 changes feedback), and look for pull — not praise.

Failed launches are expensive teachers. But they're only wasted if you don't change how you build next time.

I shut down my first startup last month.

It hurts. It also taught me more than any job, course, or book ever could.

Here are the lessons I am carrying forward:

1. Fall in love with the problem, not your solution.

We built features customers politely liked but never urgently needed. If people are not pulling the product out of your hands, you do not have product-market fit yet, no matter how polished the demo looks.

2. Talk to customers every single week.

Our best insights never came from dashboards. They came from awkward, honest conversations where someone told us exactly why they churned. I wish I had scheduled those calls before writing a single line of code, and never stopped.

3. Cash is oxygen.

We treated fundraising like a milestone instead of a lifeline, and we spent as if the next round was guaranteed. It was not. Every hire and every tool should have earned its keep.

4. Hire slowly, decide quickly.

A small team of people who trust each other and move fast will beat a larger team waiting for perfect clarity. I kept some hard decisions waiting for months. Everyone knew. It cost us momentum we could not spare.

5. Your health is part of the business.

I ignored sleep, exercise, and family and called it dedication. Burnout did not make me sharper. It made me reactive, defensive, and worse at the very judgment calls the company needed most from me.

I am proud of what we built and grateful to our team, our customers, and everyone who believed in us early.

Five years ago, I started managing a fully remote engineering team across four time zones. I thought great remote leadership was mostly about tools: Slack, standups, and a good wiki.

I was wrong. Here are three lessons that actually changed how we work:

1. Write it down, or it didn't happen.
Remote teams don't fail from lack of talent. They fail from decisions buried in calls and DMs. We moved to async-first updates, clear RFCs, and decision logs. Writing forced clarity, reduced meetings, and gave quieter engineers an equal voice.

2. Trust is built in small, consistent moments.
You can't manage by walking around when there's no office. What works: reliable 1:1s, public praise, private feedback delivered quickly, and never surprising someone in a performance review. Psychological safety isn't a slogan. It's whether people raise risks early, when fixing them is still cheap.

3. Clarity beats availability.
Being online 12 hours a day didn't make me a better manager. Clear goals, clear owners, and clear definitions of done did. When priorities are explicit, people don't need to chase approvals across time zones. They can do deep work and log off.

The biggest shift? I stopped measuring presence and started measuring outcomes, energy, and trust.

Remote doesn't make good management harder. It makes weak management more visible — and good management more scalable.

We still get plenty wrong, but revisiting these three habits every quarter has kept the team healthy, focused, and remarkably low on drama.

One year ago, I became a manager for the first time.

I thought the job was about having answers. It turns out, it's mostly about asking better questions.

Here are a few lessons that changed how I work:

1. Your calendar is your strategy. If my week is full of reacting, I'm not leading. Protecting time to think, prepare, and follow up isn't selfish — it's the work.

2. Clear is kind. Vague feedback doesn't spare feelings; it creates anxiety. Specific, timely, and honest is far more respectful than comfortable and unclear.

3. Don't solve too quickly. My instinct was to fix every problem brought to me. Now I ask, "What do you think we should do?" first. People grow when they own the answer.

4. Trust is built in small moments. Doing what you said you'd do. Admitting a mistake quickly. Listening without checking your phone. None of it is dramatic. All of it matters.

5. You can't pour from an empty cup. Burnout doesn't make you a better leader. It makes you a shorter-tempered one. Rest is part of the job, too.

I'm still learning, still getting plenty wrong. But I'm grateful for a team that gave me grace while I figured it out.

To my fellow first-time managers: you don't need to be perfect. You need to be present, consistent, and willing to learn in public.
